Feature
A Feature is the abstraction of a real-world phenomenon, according to ISO 19109:2015, Geo -
graphic information — Rules for application schemas. Features may represent tangible objects 
in the world, such as roads and buildings; or conceptual objects with no physical form such as 
administrative regions. A Feature is described in terms of its characteristics or properties, which 
can be spatial, such as position or extent; or non-spatial, such as name, identifier, density, or 
mass. A ‘Feature Type’ is a class of real-world objects having a common set of properties rep -
resented by attributes and associations; whereas a ‘Feature Instance’ is a uniquely identifiable, 
individual member of the Feature Type. Note that the term Feature may be used to denote either 
one of the more specific terms: Feature Instance or Feature Type (see [ISO 19101-1:2014]); in 
contexts where only one or the other meaning is relevant, the more specific term should be used.

1 Introduction
1.1 Purpose 
The purpose of this document is to describe the KSA National Feature Concept Dictionary con-
taining both Foundation Themes and Feature Concepts which will be used within the Kingdom. 
It also describes how the dictionary elements (Foundation Themes and Feature Concepts) can 
be managed as they evolve over time to meet the Kingdom’s needs. This document is a National 
Standard and is based on standards developed by the International Organization for Standard-
ization (ISO).
1.2 Scope 
This document covers the structure and maintenance process for the KSA Feature Concept 
Dictionary. It defines the structure of the dictionary elements (Foundation Themes and Feature 
Concepts). It specifies how the Register can be managed and accessed and it also documents 
the following Registers: 
• Foundation Themes agreed as part of the Data Governance process.
• Proposed Feature Concepts required to support the Logical Data Model for each 
Foundation Theme.
• These Registers, once fully approved by the Control Body, will then be managed in the Fea-
ture Concept Dictionary Registry.

This document does apply additional provisions as it applies ISO 19135 to the scope of the KSA 
Feature Concept Dictionary. 
This document is applicable to Data Producers that provide geospatial data and metadata for 
the Foundation Themes.

Stepwise evolution in which prioritized elements are implemented on an ‘as-needed basis’ is

1.3.1 Goals of a Feature Concept Dictionary
A Feature Concept Dictionary (FCD) contains a list of identified, common terms and descrip-
tions that support the definition of Feature Types across all Foundation Themes. It also ensures 
consistency in the ongoing development of Feature Types as the Foundation Themes evolve. 
A Feature Concept Dictionary defines two artefacts: 
• Foundation Themes which represent logical groupings of geospatial concepts. Example 
Foundation Themes include ‘Land Use’, ‘Transport’, etc. 
• Feature Concepts. These are typically grouped within a Foundation Theme and provide a 
conceptual basis for realizable Feature Type descriptions. Examples of Feature Concepts are 
‘Farm’ and ‘Road’

Feature Concepts. These are typically grouped within a Foundation Theme and provide a 
conceptual basis for realizable Feature Type descriptions. Examples of Feature Concepts are 
‘Farm’ and ‘Road’ 
• The Foundation Theme and Feature Concept Dictionary support the following National Spa-
tial Data Infrastructure requirements:

6
• Discovery. Understanding the content of the geospatial information of the nation in a con-
sistent format. By classifying data products with relevant Foundation Themes and Feature 
Concepts within metadata, it is possible to identify relevant Foundation data more easily 
• Harmonization. Supporting harmonization efforts by identifying similarities and differences 
between the Features in different geospatial Datasets and across Foundation Themes 
• Management. Foundation Themes in particular support the organization of the nation’s geo-
spatial data into clear groupings, thereby allowing the effective collaboration of Custodians 
and creation of data that can be used by a wide community
It is important to note that:
. The FCD will be incrementally developed as the Foundation Themes are being de-
veloped
. Feature Concepts within the Feature Concept Dictionary are continually evolving 
throughout the life of the Foundation Themes
1.4 Structure and Processes of a Feature Concept Dictionary
A key aspect of Feature Concepts is that they have a well-defined name, a clear description and 
have a life cycle managed by a version-controlled Register (i.e.

cesses of a Feature Concept Dictionary
A key aspect of Feature Concepts is that they have a well-defined name, a clear description and 
have a life cycle managed by a version-controlled Register (i.e. they are persistent and managed).
The KSA Feature Concept Dictionary consists of two Registers, the National Foundation Theme 
Register and the National Feature Concept Register as shown in Figure 1. Additional Registers 
may be added at a later date. 
Note that the term Dictionary and Register are used interchangeably in many specifications. 
Although the generic term Feature Concept Dictionary is often used, in formal terms this spec-
ification describes two Register types and instances of those Registers.
A Register (ISO 19135:2015) in this case can be considered a subset of a Dictionary where the 
items adhere to formal registration procedures. Items in the Register have a unique identifi-
er, a clear description and a well-defined lifecycle with an audit trail (when they were created, 
modified and retired - they are never deleted). In addition, items also have versions so the state 
of the item at any point in time is available.

3 KS A Foundation Theme Characteristics
3.1 Overview
Geospatial Foundation Themes provide a key set of classifications allowing the identification, 
harmonization and management of geospatial data. Foundation Themes have a strong relation-
ship to the quality of life (QoL) groups of the country. Many nations and inter-governmental 
organizations (e.g. the UN and European Union) have defined a set of Foundation Themes.
A set of Foundation Themes defined to meet the requirements of the Kingdom have been agreed. 
While referred to sometimes simply as ‘Themes’, the Foundation Theme Register deals with primarily 
‘Foundation Themes’. This is a set of Themes which cover the necessary scope of geospatial data for all the 
countries requirements.

‘Foundation Themes’. This is a set of Themes which cover the necessary scope of geospatial data for all the 
countries requirements. It is possible to define other sets of Themes (often known as Additional or Sup-
plementary Themes) to cover the requirements of specific domains by offering additional/alternative clas-
sifications. If these Themes are formal, they should follow the structure and processes in this document.

Foundation Themes consist of the following elements (necessary to meet the requirements of 
ISO19135-1) together with additional KSA specific required properties:
• Foundation Theme Identifier (must be unique, required by ISO19135:2015)
• Foundation Theme Name (added to meet the requirements of KSA)
• Foundation Theme Description (added to meet the requirements of KSA)
• Status (required by ISO19135:2015 Lifecycle code)
• Foundation Theme submitted, validated, invalidated, superseded and retired dates 
(required by ISO19135:2015).
• Source information (identification of the origin of the description). (Added to meet

3.3 Methodology for Developing Foundation Themes 
The Foundation Themes and their descriptions are developed at a national level and coordinated 
by the National Regulator. The Foundation Theme methodology takes into account International 
Best Practice established by UN-GGIM, ANZLIC etc., and is described in detail in the National 
Governance Framework reference document [ 7].
3.4 Use of Multiple Languages When Defining Foundation Themes
ISO 19135 supports the creation of Registers that support multiple languages. Each Foundation 
Theme shall include a single identifier, a name defined in both English and Arabic, and a defini-
tion defined in both English and Arabic.
3.5 Dealing with Data That Falls Outside of a Foundation Theme
In many cases, Custodians of Foundation Themes will be asked to classify information in terms 
of what Foundation Theme(s) it relates to (for example by referencing one or more relevant 
Foundation Themes in the metadata of a dataset). 
As KSA is initially adopting 12 Foundation Themes necessary to describe the geospatial Foun-
dation Data of the country, allowing Custodians to state clearly that they have not found a Foun-

taset). 
As KSA is initially adopting 12 Foundation Themes necessary to describe the geospatial Foun-
dation Data of the country, allowing Custodians to state clearly that they have not found a Foun-
dation Theme relevant to KSA, is an important element. As a result, an additional registered 
pseudo-theme called ‘Other’ has been added. This is to allow a Custodian to classify data as not 
being relevant to an existing Foundation Theme, and support the identification of a gap which 
will need to be filled by revising the content of the Foundation Theme Register, either by de-
fining a new Foundation Theme or by broadening the scope of an existing Foundation Theme.
4 KS A Feature Concept Characteristics 
4.1 Overview
KSA Feature Concepts provide a key set of classifications allowing for the identification, harmo-
nization and management of geospatial data. Feature Concepts in the Feature Concept Register 
each reference the Foundation Theme which defines how they are managed.
A Feature Concept is a general representation of a Feature type (ISO 19126), which means that it 
defines something without specifying any implementation restrictions (whereas a Feature Type

anaged.
A Feature Concept is a general representation of a Feature type (ISO 19126), which means that it 
defines something without specifying any implementation restrictions (whereas a Feature Type 
has specific properties and constraints).
The Feature Concept must fit within the scope of the Foundation Theme, for example for a 
depth contour to be added to the ‘Elevation’ Theme, the Elevation Theme scope must include 
the Earth’s surface above and below sea-level.
Foundation Theme requirements have been reviewed, International Best Practice consulted, 
and a set of initial Feature Concepts have been developed. Feature Concepts are candidates 
(submitted) until approved by the control body. Further submissions will be considered from 
KSA Custodians as the FCD becomes operational.

Feature Concepts consist of the following properties (necessary to meet the requirements of 
ISO19135-1 and KSA Specific additions).
1. Feature Concept Identifier (must be unique, ISO19135 requirement)
2. Feature Concept Name (added to meet the requirements of KSA)
3. Feature Concept Description (ISO19135 requirement)

4.3 Methodology for Developing Feature Concepts
Feature Concepts are developed within the Foundation Themes by submitting organizations 
(the Foundation Theme Working Groups). The process is summarized as follows:
• Identify that there is a deficiency in the Feature Concepts registered. Identify the KSA data 
requirement which leads to this deficiency.
• Review best practice internationally to identify if a similar Concept has been defined elsewhere.
• Consider the merits of existing descriptions and form a description (new or drawn from best 
practice) relevant to KSA requirements. 
• Submit the request to the Feature Concept Register Manager.
• Engage with the National Regulator to formalize the Feature Concept.

Scope and Objectives of the Guideline 
 
The purpose of this Guideline is to set out the minimum requirements for the determination of one -, two- or 
three-dimensional position, parameters of Earth gravity potential field, their temporal variations, and associated 
accuracies of survey control marks in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. 
 
This Guideline prescribes requirements for control surveys that define, extend, improve, densify, or otherwise 
connect to the SANSRS. The control surveys can be conducted in 1D (vertical only), 2D (horizontal only), or 3D 
(both horizontal and vertical). T he following control surveys are within the scope of this Guideline – Geodetic 
Datum Control Surveys and General-Purpose Control Surveys. These surveys are defined below. 
 
Geodetic Datum Control Surveys define, extend, or improve the SANSRS. These control surveys are included in 
the SANSRS network adjustments to allow for the most rigorous estimation and testing of position and accuracy 
for new and existing survey control marks.

2.1 Quantifying Accuracy 
2.1.1 Accuracy Classification (GEOSA Conventions) 
Accuracy is defined as the level of closeness of an estimated value – measured or computed – of a quantity to its 
true or accepted value. 
 
Current GEOSA conventions classify the accuracy of National Control Networks and their individual geodetic 
reference points according to Class and Order. 
 
2.1.1.1 Class 
 
The assignment of Class is based on the accuracy (as defined in Section 2.1.1) of a geodetic reference point and 
the consistency of that geodetic reference point with other geodetic reference points within the network. Thus: 
• A geodetic reference point of a certain Class is consistent with all other geodetic reference points of the 
same Class within the network and its associated reference frame. 
• A geodetic reference point of a certain Class is consistent with, and of the same Class as all other 
geodetic reference point within the survey(s) that established the geodetic reference point. 
 
2.1.1.2 Order 
 
The assignment of Order is not directly related to the accuracy of a geodetic reference point . The order is

t within the survey(s) that established the geodetic reference point. 
 
2.1.1.2 Order 
 
The assignment of Order is not directly related to the accuracy of a geodetic reference point . The order is 
assigned based on the contribution of a geodetic reference point to the formation of the network and the 
propagation of the associated reference frame. Thus: 
• A geodetic reference point considered high accuracy (e.g. Class 1) and that provides a minimal 
contribution to the propagation of the reference frame (e.g. a small -scale deformation monitoring 
network) would be assigned a low order. 
• A geodetic reference point considered medium accu racy (e.g. Class 2) and that is critical to the 
propagation of the reference frame (e.g. a leveling junction point) would be assigned a high order.

2.1.2.1 Definition 
 
The accuracy of a parameter (e.g. 3D position, physical height) is quantified by a nu merical value (with 
appropriate SI units) representing the 95% confidence level of the parameter. The parameter that the accuracy 
is associated with is assumed to be free of gross and systematic errors. 
 
2.1.2.2 Local Accuracy 
 
The accuracy of a parameter (e.g. 3D position of a geodetic reference point) is relative to the survey in which it 
was observed, free from the influence of any imprecision or inaccuracy in the underlying reference frame. 
Therefore, local accuracy reflects only the accuracy resulting from survey measurements, measurement 
precisions, network geometry, and the choice of constraints. 
 
2.1.2.3 Network Accuracy 
 
The accuracy of a parameter (e.g. 3D position of a geodetic reference point) with respect to the defined reference 
frame. Network accuracy represents the combined accuracy of the existing reference frame realization and the 
new survey. That is, network accuracy includes local accuracy as well as the accuracy of the existing survey control

esents the combined accuracy of the existing reference frame realization and the 
new survey. That is, network accuracy includes local accuracy as well as the accuracy of the existing survey control 
marks to which a new control survey is connected. 
 
2.1.2.4 Implementation 
 
A least squares adjustment must be used to estimate and test survey accuracy. For local accuracy , a minimally 
constrained adjustment must be used. For network accuracy a fully constrained adjustment must be used, 
however, the control should not be fixed, but rather constrained using the variance matrix from the national 
adjustment. 
 
Both local and network accuracies should be provided in appropriate SI units at the 95% confidence level. 
 
Local accuracy for horizontal and vertical geodetic control points is similar to the current GEOSA accuracy 
methodology using the Class system since they both describe the relative accuracy between points. Hence, the 
current Class methodology can be converted into local accuracy by taking the average length of the line, using 
the currently defined accuracy of the points, and converting that into a value in meters.

2.3.1 KSA-CORS Network 
2.3.1.1 Definition 
 
The KSA-CORS Network is a network of GNSS Continuously Operating Reference Stations ( CORS) that serves as 
the primary connection of KSA -GRF17 to the International Terrestrial Reference Frame (ITRF). The KSA -CORS 
Network is an example of an Acti ve National Geodetic Network (Active NGN) and, as such, it physically realizes 
KSA-GRF17 throughout the KSA. 
 
Each CORS within the KSA -CORS Network continuously tracks and observes signals from all available GNSS 
satellites. The resulting observation data is streamed (in real-time) to centralized computing facilities where the 
data is processed to generate products and services that support a wide variety of post-processed and real-time 
positioning applications at the centimeter level.

The observation data continuously accumulated from the KSA -CORS Network is critical to the development, 
propagation, and maintenance of the KSA-GRF17. Similarly, the real-time services generated from the KSA-CORS 
Network play a pivotal role in providing end-users with access to the KSA-GRF17.

The 3D position of a KSA -CORS must be realized in KSA -GRF17 using GNSS measurement techniques, network 
adjustment, and existing KSA-CORS. 
• The GNSS measurement and network adjustment techniques utilized must conform with at least the

• The 3D position must be derived from at least three existing KSA-CORS using GNSS observation data of 
at least one week in duration (7 days x 24 hours) as recommended in the IBP reference of ICSM CORS 
guidelines. 
• The 3D position must be accompanied by evidence that the accuracy requirements ( Section 2.3.1.5) 
have been met.

2.3.4.6.2 Special Events 
 
A special event is defined as any occurrence that could reasonably be considered to impact the value of absolute

2.4.1.4.1 GNSS Survey Methodology

will depend on the type of survey carried out – static baseline or PPP . 
 
In the case of a static baseline, the typical steps in the processing include: 
• Importing data from two or more receivers, 
• Identifying reference and rover receivers and fixing the coordinates of the reference, 
• Pre-processing (e.g. cycle slip detection, outlier rejection, etc.), 
• Baseline formation, 
• Ambiguity resolution, 
• Position computation, 
• Achieved accuracy estimation, 
• Quality control checks.

In the case of PPP , the typical process is as follows:

• Ambiguity resolution (optional), 
• Position computation, 
• Achieved accuracy estimation,

2.4.3 GNSS/Leveling Surveys 
2.4.3.1 Introduction 
 
GNSS/leveling is a height determination method based on static GNSS observations and a geoid model. 
 
As shown in Section 2.4.1, GNSS can observe heights to an accuracy of <20mm using Static methods. Whilst 
conventional geodetic leveling can be used to observe heights to millimeter-level accuracy over short distances, 
this error increases with distance, whereas GNSS errors remain largely the same over distances of up to a few 
tens of kilometers. On a medium scale, both techniques achieve comparable accuracy. 
 
GNSS can only provide ellipsoidal height differences (h), so in order to compute orthometric heights (H), a geoid 
ellipsoid separation (N) must be applied. 
 
In KSA, in order to perform GNSS/leveling, the following conditions must be met: 
• GNSS observations need to be taken using the Static method. 
• GNSS observations need to be processed to yield KSA-GRF17 ellipsoidal height differences.

ing, the following conditions must be met: 
• GNSS observations need to be taken using the Static method. 
• GNSS observations need to be processed to yield KSA-GRF17 ellipsoidal height differences. 
• KSA-GEOID21 needs to be used as the geoid model. 
 
2.4.3.2 Accuracy Aspects 
 
The accuracy of a GNSS/leveling survey depends on: 
- Accuracy of the Static GNSS survey and resultant ellipsoidal height difference. 
- (Relative) accuracy of the gravimetric geoid model. 
The first factor can be derived from the network adjustment statistics of the GNSS survey. The second is not as 
easy to determine, as combined hybrid geoid models such as KSA-GEOID21 are affected by several compounding 
errors. Geoid model accuracy varies depending on geographic location, quality, coverage, and density of available 
gravity data, terrain variations, and the regularity of the geoid.

2.5.2 Tide Gauge Station (TG) 
 
A tide gauge is a system for observing the height of the sea level relative to the height of the land. Tide gauges

2.5.3 Space Geodetic Stations 
Apart from GNSS, other space geodetic techniques such as Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI), Satellite 
Laser Ranging (SLR), and Doppler Orbitography and Radio-positioning Integrated by Satellite (DORIS) can help to 
contribute to the realization of th e International Terrestrial Reference Frame (ITRF), monitoring of the Earth 
rotation, and monitoring of the motions of tectonic plates. 
 
Currently, KSA does not have any VLBI, SLR, or DORIS stations, however, in the future one or more of these 
stations may be built. If/when this happens, these guidelines will need to be updated to reflect that change. 
 
A short description of each technique is provided below. 
 
2.5.3.1 Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) 
 
SLR is used to measure the time of flight of a laser to reach a satellite and return to the Earth. The technique can 
be used to uniquely define the Earth’s center of mass and, along with VLBI, the scale of the Earth. It is also used 
to help compute Earth Orientation Parameters (EOPs) of polar motion (pole coordinates) and the rapid variations 
in length-of-day (LoD).

and, along with VLBI, the scale of the Earth. It is also used 
to help compute Earth Orientation Parameters (EOPs) of polar motion (pole coordinates) and the rapid variations 
in length-of-day (LoD). SLR is also the most accurate way to resolve the center of satellites which helps to calibrate 
radar altimeters and separate long-term instrumentation drift from secular changes in ocean topography. 
 
2.5.3.2 Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) 
 
Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) is a technique that detects radio transmissions from extragalactic radio 
sources. Using the difference in time at which the signals from the source arrive at different radio telescopes, it 
is possible to determine EOPs, Universal time (UT1), polar motion (pole coordinates), and precession and 
nutation. Along with SLR, VLBI is also used to measure the scale of the Earth. 
 
2.5.3.3 Doppler Orbitography and Radio-positioning Integrated by Satellite (DORIS) 
 
DORIS is a system that can determine the distance between a ground statio n and a satellite. It is based on 
accurate measurements of the Doppler shifts on a radiofrequency signal emitted by ground stations and received

t can determine the distance between a ground statio n and a satellite. It is based on 
accurate measurements of the Doppler shifts on a radiofrequency signal emitted by ground stations and received 
onboard different satellites carrying DORIS receivers. A ground segment monitors and processes the data and 
scientific products distributed by the International DORIS Service. Since the position of the ground stations is 
known, DORIS allows precise determination of the satellite orbits. 
 
2.6 Geodetic Earth Observation (GEO) Techniques 
Geodetic Earth Observation (GEO) techniques include satellite gravimetry and altimetry that have been actively 
used for various aspects of SANSRS definition, as well as emerging techniques such as Interferometric Synthetic 
Aperture Radar (InSAR) that can be used to measure deformation at a local scale. 
 
Guidelines for these techniques are not as mature as other geodetic techniques described in . For this reason, 
these techniques are only briefly described in this section.

2.6.1 Satellite Gravimetry 
Satellite gravimetry utilizes the principle of interacting masses, those being, in this case, the mass of the Earth 
and that of an orbiting satellite. This interaction causes perturbations of the satellite orbit which can be measured 
in order to draw conclusions about the gravitational forces acting on the satellite. 
The main observation principles for satellite gravimetry are: 
• Satellite-to-satellite tracking in high -low mode: A Low Earth Orbiting (LEO) satellite is tracked by high 
orbiting GNSS satellites, relative to a network of ground stations. The LEO satellite is a probe within the 
Earth’s gravity field, which can be precisely tracked without interruption. The observed 3D accelerations 
correspond to the gravity accelerations. The non -gravitational fo rces acting on the satellite are 
measured by accelerometers and accounted for.

Technical guidelines for Geodesy Page 53 of 63 
 
• Satellite-to-satellite tracking in low-low mode: Two LEO satellites are placed in the same orbit, separated 
by several hundred kilometers, and the distance between them is meas ured with the highest possible 
accuracy. Acceleration differences between the two satellites are measured by changes in the inter -
satellite distance. The two satellites can be considered as one instrument in which (1) Variations in the 
gravity field cause variations in the range between the two satellites. Areas of stronger gravity affect the 
lead satellite first and accelerate it away from the second satellite, (2) Range variations are measured 
by high-accuracy microwave link or laser-ranging interferometry, (3) The observed range variations are 
corrected for non -gravitational effects by precise accelerometers. This method provides higher 
sensitivity than the previous one. 
• Satellite gravity gradiometry : Acceleration differences in all three dimensions are m easured directly 
within a LEO satellite using an on-board gradiometer. One important advantage is that non-gravitational

gravity gradiometry : Acceleration differences in all three dimensions are m easured directly 
within a LEO satellite using an on-board gradiometer. One important advantage is that non-gravitational 
accelerations are the same for all measurements inside the satellite and hence vanish by differentiation. 
Data provided by satellite gravity field missions are essential for the determination of the Earth’s gravity 
field, the computation of global and regional geoids, the unification of vertical datums, and the 
establishment of global and national VRFs (Global Geodetic Observing System, GGOS, 2023). 
 
2.6.2 Satellite Altimetry 
Satellite altimetry is a technique for measuring the distance between an orbiting satellite and the instantaneous 
sea surface using the transition of microwave pulses in the radar frequency domain or laser pulses in the optical 
or infrared domain. Since the satellite’s altitude is known, the sea surface height can be derived as the height of 
the instantaneous sea surface above the reference ellipsoid. 
 
The main contribution of satellite altimetry is the ability to map large ocean areas within a short time period to

d as the height of 
the instantaneous sea surface above the reference ellipsoid. 
 
The main contribution of satellite altimetry is the ability to map large ocean areas within a short time period to 
obtain a representation of the sea surface with high spatial and temporal resolution. Current satellite altimetry 
missions provide sea surface heights with an accuracy of about 1 – 2 cm for a single measurement. 
 
2.6.3 Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) 
Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) is a geodetic method for detecting Earth surface displacements. 
It measures crustal changes related to geological phenomena like tectonic shifts and seismic activity. Additionally, 
it can detect ground subsidence due to activities such as groundwater extraction. 
 
InSAR provides a way to observe ground surface deformation over small local areas very precisely. Given that 
this type of deformation can be highly variable, and is often non-linear, it cannot be adequately monitored using 
sparse GNSS stations. However, if InSAR is integrated with GNSS observations, it can achieve high spatial

on can be highly variable, and is often non-linear, it cannot be adequately monitored using 
sparse GNSS stations. However, if InSAR is integrated with GNSS observations, it can achieve high spatial 
resolution, enabling the identification of surface movements at scales ranging from millimeters to centimeters. 
 
InSAR is cur rently not used in KSA for SANSRS definition or maintenance, however, it could be included in the 
future, in which case this Guideline will need to be updated. 
 
2.7 Network Adjustment – General Principles 
2.7.1 Purpose 
For geodetic control surveys, the lea st squares adjustment technique provides a reliable means for estimating 
the most probable survey control mark coordinates and accuracies from a redundant set of measurements by 
applying well-understood and agreed functional and stochastic models. The tech nique of least squares also 
provides a rigorous means for statistically testing and validating the estimated coordinates and the 
measurements used to derive them, thereby allowing the detection and elimination of measurement outliers.

2.7.2 Recommended Procedures 
Control surveys undertaken to derive the horizontal and vertical position of survey control marks relative to 
SANSRS should be adjusted using a rigorous least squares adjustment process. The following procedures are 
recommended:

(a) All survey control measurements should be corrected using known calibration parameters and other 
systematic errors accounted for. Measurements should be accompanied by reliable values of uncertainty 
(standard deviations). To test a control survey for error s, sufficient redundant measurements must be 
incorporated into the survey control network. Increased redundancy (quantified by the degrees of 
freedom in the network) leads to increased confidence in the testing results. 
(b) A minimally constrained adjustme nt should be performed and tested using the local test (see Section 
2.7.3.1) and global test (see Section 2.7.3.2) to remove outliers and validate the appropriateness of the 
stochastic model. If the stochastic model is deemed inappropriate, the stochastic model should be 
corrected (e.g. by scaling) before continuing. 
(c) The uncertainty of the least squares outputs (e.g. coordinates) should be examined to assess whether the 
survey has achieved any predefined thresholds. 
(d) Once an acceptable minimally constrained adjustment has been completed, a fully constrained

coordinates) should be examined to assess whether the 
survey has achieved any predefined thresholds. 
(d) Once an acceptable minimally constrained adjustment has been completed, a fully constrained 
adjustment, using appropriately weighted constraints, must be performed. The fully constrained 
adjustment must not use “fixed” constraints or “known values” to assign infinite (or other inappropriate) 
weights. 
(e) The fully constrained adjustment should be tested using the local test (see Section 2.7.3.1), to verify that 
the imposed constraints do not result in measurement failure(s). 
(f) The fully constrained adjustment should be tested using the global test (see Section 2.7.3.2 ). If this 
adjustment test fails, the constraints need to be examined to identify and rectify the cause of failure. 
(g) The uncertainty of the least squares outputs (e.g. coordinates) should be examined to assess whether the 
survey has achieved any predefined thresholds.

2.7.3 Statistical Testing 
Statistical tests in a network adjustment are used to identify and eliminate measurement outliers, validate the 
stochastic model applied to the measurements, and assess and/or demonstrate the overall accuracy of a survey 
control network. The following two tests should be under taken on both minimally constrained and fully 
constrained adjustments. 
2.7.3.1 Local Test 
 
The local test is an evaluation procedure performed on individual survey measurements to assess the quality of 
a measurement and its assumed ( apriori) standard deviation. This is done by assessing the magnitude of each 
measurement correction against an appropriate test statistic (such as the normalized residual) at an appropriate 
confidence interval (usually 95%). Such testing should be undertaken to demonstrate that: 
• Any gross errors within the measurement set are identified and eliminated. 
• All measurements are appropriately weighted. 
• In the case of constrained adjustment, the imposed constraints do not put undue strain on the 
measurements. 
2.7.3.2 Global Test

• All measurements are appropriately weighted. 
• In the case of constrained adjustment, the imposed constraints do not put undue strain on the 
measurements. 
2.7.3.2 Global Test 
 
The global test assesses the quality of the survey as a whole. A single test statistic is computed and assessed at 
an appropriate confidence level (usually 95% confidence). Statistical failure of the global test indicates either the 
presence of significant outliers and/or an inappropriate stochastic model has been applied to the measurements.

Refer to Section 2.1 for information on the conventions used by GEOSA to express the accuracy of a least squares 
adjustment.

2.2 Emerging Conditions & their Influence on the Geospatial Ecosystem
The Geospatial Ecosystem is undergoing a profound transformation, driven by a convergence 
of emerging technologies, evolving user expectations, and new sources of data. As spatial 
information becomes increasingly embedded in everyday decision-making, the need to 
understand and adapt to these changes is more critical than ever. Some of the key conditions 
shaping the future of Geospatial systems and their far-reaching influence across industries 
and society are listed below:
1. Technological Advancements
The Geospatial Ecosystem is being reshaped by rapid technological progress. Devices are 
becoming faster, smaller, and smarter, forming interconnected networks of IoT sensors that 
continuously generate spatial data. Cloud computing enables scalable spatial analytics, 
while edge computing supports real-time decision-making. Enhanced communication 
infrastructure, including satellite-based internet and the potential of quantum communication,

is expanding global connectivity. Devices now possess spatial awareness, allowing them to 
locate and contextualize themselves. As this Geospatial Ecosystem evolves, it is essential to 
design sustainable, efficient architectures that embed privacy and data protection at their 
core.
2. Location in Decision-Making
Location data is increasingly central to informed decision-making. With approximately 80% 
of all data containing a spatial component, governments and businesses are leveraging it 
across domains such as climate change, energy distribution, water supply, geopolitics, and 
socioeconomic planning. Locally, Geospatial insights support daily operations and evidence-
based decisions. The COVID-19 pandemic underscored the value of location data in managing 
social distancing, delivering essential services, and coordinating vaccine distribution.

Advances in automation and analytics are transforming Geospatial workflows. Machines now 
autonomously process real-time spatial data, with voice and visual interfaces increasingly 
replacing traditional input methods. Semantic tools are being integrated into Geospatial 
processing, enabling contextual understanding. The rise of Geospatial digital twins combined 
with AI/ML models, is enhancing predictive capabilities. Open Science initiatives are fostering 
collaborative research, improving efficiency and transparency through shared data and 
methodologies.
4. Evolving User Expectations
The mainstreaming of spatiotemporal data has led to diverse user needs. With immersive 
visualization tools and scalable processing services, users from digital natives to institutional 
stakeholders expect intuitive, fast, and accessible Geospatial solutions. Governments and 
enterprises alike demand simplified interfaces and actionable insights. Virtual analytic 
workbenches, accessible via web platforms, emerge as essential tools to meet these 
expectations.

5. Changing Organizational Structures
To stay relevant, organizations must evolve. Agility, continuous learning, and cross-functional

adjacent industries, broadening the application of spatial data. Organizational adaptability in 
structure and strategy is vital for long-term relevance.

The Geospatial data landscape is diversifying. Private companies now contribute valuable 
content alongside National Mapping Agencies (NMAs). Initiatives like Copernicus offer free 
Earth observation data, while specialized services refine this data into high-resolution 3D 
models using cost-effective technologies such as UAV mounted imaging and LiDAR sensors.

frequently. Various stakeholders shape and coordinate the Geospatial Ecosystem and

Vision
The Saudi Arabian Geospatial Ecosystem is the Saudi Arabian sustainable, active, and 
nationally relevant Geospatial Ecosystem that contributes to all activities and applications 
that require any element of Geospatial knowledge through an interconnected Geospatial 
Ecosystem of people, policies, practices, and procedures addressing the needs of the 
modern world.
Mission
The Geospatial Ecosystem provides a ubiquitous network of interconnected Geospatial 
information, products, technology, and services, enabling the delivery of knowledge-based 
insights to facilitate a bottom-up approach to problem-solving and decision-making.
Objectives
The goals of the Geospatial Ecosystem go far beyond merely exchanging data. The goal is 
to create a network that provides powerful components, data, and services that directly 
address real-world problems and future what-if scenarios. At the same time, it is essential

4.1 Rationale 
The Initiative “Enable Geospatial Ecosystem Practices” is driven by the imperative to embrace 
and uphold the best Geospatial Ecosystem practices and working modalities necessary to 
sustain the interconnectedness of stakeholders within the Geospatial Ecosystem network. In 
today’s rapidly evolving world, Geospatial information facilitates informed decision-making, 
resource management, disaster response, and more. Recognizing this interconnected 
Geospatial Ecosystem’s significance, optimizing its operations, and ensuring it operates at 
its full potential is crucial.
This Initiative aims to create a harmonious environment where various stakeholders, from 
government bodies to private entities, can effectively collaborate and contribute to the 
growth of the Geospatial Ecosystem. By adopting the best practices, we can ensure the 
seamless flow of Geospatial data, information, and services, which is vital for holistic, real-
world decision-making.

Geospatial data layers in the Kingdom.

collaboration and clarity of roles.

Project 15 was initiated to establish a robust Geospatial security and regulatory framework 
within the Geospatial Ecosystem, aimed at safeguarding sensitive data, ensuring

2. Logical Consistency: This measures the degree of adherence to the logical rules of the 
national Geospatial data model. It includes:
 • Feature Consistency: Compliance with the general schema rules of the model.
 • Domain Consistency: Compliance with the values of the model’s domains.
 • Actual Consistency: The extent to which data storage adheres to the national 
Geospatial data model’s structure.
 • Topological Consistency: The validity of topological properties of the dataset.

has emerged as a foundational asset for national development, 
digital transformation, and evidence-based decision-making. 
From urban planning and infrastructure development to 
environmental monitoring and disaster response, location-
based data plays a critical role in shaping policy, delivering 
services, and driving innovation. Recognizing this, governments 
around the world are investing in Geospatial capabilities to 
improve governance, enhance public sector efficiency, and 
support sustainable development.

Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information 
Management (UN-GGIM) developed the United Nations 
Integrated Geospatial Information Framework (UN-IGIF), a 
comprehensive blueprint for strengthening national Geospatial 
information management. Formally adopted in August 2018, 
UN-IGIF provides a strategic and implementation framework

The UN-IGIF is structured around nine Strategic Pathways, which span three core domains: 
governance, technology, and people. These pathways are:
Governance and Institutions – Establishing leadership, institutional arrangements, and 
governance models to coordinate Geospatial activities.
Policy and Legal – Developing legal frameworks and policies to regulate data access, 
privacy, licensing, and sharing.
Financial – Identifying sustainable funding models and investment strategies for 
Geospatial infrastructure.
Data – Ensuring the availability, quality, and interoperability of Geospatial data through 
custodianship and supply chains.

Geospatial capabilities, identify gaps, and implement targeted reforms. The framework is 
designed to be flexible and scalable, allowing countries to tailor their implementation based 
on national priorities, institutional maturity, and available resources.
Since its adoption, UN-IGIF has gained traction globally. Many countries have initiated 
Country-Level Action Plans (CAPs) to operationalize the framework, aligning their national 
Geospatial strategies with the nine pathways. These CAPs serve as roadmaps for institutional 
reform, technical modernization, and stakeholder engagement. Developing countries 
and small island states have embraced the framework to build foundational Geospatial 
infrastructure, improve data governance, and participate in global Geospatial dialogues.

2.1 National Geospatial Policy
The national Geospatial policy framework for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia aims to ensure 
that Geospatial data are governed, protected, classified, licensed, priced, and shared in a 
manner that maximizes their value as national assets while safeguarding confidentiality, 
integrity, and public trust. The framework reflects international best practices, aligns with 
the UN-IGIF, and provides the legal and institutional foundation for sustainable Geospatial 
management in the Kingdom.

National Geospatial Data Governance Principles
The National Geospatial Regulator provides oversight, licensing, and coordination across the 
public and private sectors. Key governance principles include:
• Centralized oversight: The national mapping agency supervises all Geospatial 
foundation themes, appointing Custodians for datasets and data products.
• Single source of truth: Foundation data are collected once, continuously maintained, 
and used many times to prevent duplication and ensure consistency.
• Government ownership: All Geospatial data created by public agencies belong to the 
Saudi Arabian government.
• Licensing and compliance: The national mapping agency regulates permits for data 
production, dissemination, and commercial use, ensuring both public and private sector 
compliance.
• International data exchange: The national mapping agency is the sole authority for 
sharing national data with international Geospatial platforms.
• Accountability: Data producers retain responsibility for accuracy, while the national

These governance principles establish a clear chain of accountability and protect both 
government and commercial interests, ensuring that Geospatial information remains a 
strategic national asset.
National Geospatial Data Classification
Recognizing the need to balance openness with security, a four-tier data classification 
system is applied: Highly Confidential, Confidential, Restricted, and Public.
• By default, data is public, unless sensitivity requires restrictions.
• Classification decisions must be timely and proportional to potential risks.
• Custodians and producers apply varying levels of classification, with the national 
mapping agency retaining final authority on very confidential and public categories.
This classification system ensures that sensitive datasets remain secure while maximizing 
the availability of public Geospatial data to stimulate innovation and research.

National Geospatial Data Licensing 
Licensing is an instrument to define and apply specific rights of use in specific 
circumstances to a specific work, including Geospatial data. The license specifically 
distinguishes the rights of use, which may be granted to the licensee, from the proprietary 
rights held by the licensor, and includes an explicit statement with regard to the related data.
There are three types of Geospatial data licensing, which are:
1. Viewing license (viewing)
2. Use license (access and use)
3. Production license (for derivative data or applications)

3.1 National Geospatial Data Pricing
Geospatial information and data are considered national wealth that all government agencies 
must develop. Government agencies must guarantee the preservation of Geospatial 
information and data as national assets, and every government agency that produces data 
must retain the intellectual property rights to that data. Any government agency has the 
right to develop its products from national Geospatial data, in accordance with Geospatial 
policies. National agencies have development rights within the framework of intellectual 
property in accordance with relevant laws and regulations.
The basic principles for Geospatial data pricing are as follows:
• Government agencies have the right to share products based on national Geospatial 
data in exchange for financial compensation.
• Government agencies have the right to price data or data products at less than the 
estimated cost price to support other goals such as economic development or national 
security.
• Geospatial data is exchanged between government agencies free of charge.

19109) and international best practices, aligning with efforts of

on Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM), the

Purpose and Objective of NGMP
The NGMP was designed to:
• Standardize how metadata is documented for Geospatial datasets and services in Saudi 
Arabia.
• Ensure consistency across Custodians, minimizing duplication and enhancing 
discoverability.
• Provide the foundation for a federated catalogue system where datasets can be 
searched and accessed by stakeholders across government, academia, private sector, 
and the public.
• Support compliance with data governance regulations.
At its core, the NGMP ensures that every dataset carries a uniform description of content, 
quality, lineage, spatial and temporal coverage, and custodianship. This makes datasets 
more reliable for reuse and helps avoid the inefficiencies of siloed, inconsistent metadata 
practices.

address national priorities. The extensions cover:

The comprehensive framework for Geospatial data standards plays a pivotal role in

Geospatial Data Quality
At the core of the Geospatial standards lies an emphasis on Geospatial data quality 
management. Recognizing that Geospatial data inherently contains uncertainty

Central to this approach is ISO 19157:2023, which provides a structured method for evaluating 
data quality through elements such as completeness, positional accuracy, thematic quality, 
logical consistency, and temporal validity. Under the governance model, each dataset must 
conform to a formal specification approved by a national body, which in turn enables the 
generation of quantitative quality metrics.
Complementing this, concepts from the W3C Data Quality Vocabulary (DQV), support multi-
dimensional descriptions of data quality. This enables both producers and users to evaluate 
datasets flexibly according to their own needs, a crucial requirement as data moves beyond 
traditional business-to-business (B2B) exchanges into broader business-to-consumer (B2C)

Quality assurance is further strengthened with metaquality indicators—such as confidence,

a national data quality model has been developed, complete with standardized evaluation

Geospatial Data Quality Evaluation
In addition to defining standards, systematic evaluation methods are prescribed for 
assessing Geospatial data quality. These methods are classified as direct and indirect:
• Direct evaluation inspects the dataset itself, comparing it against reference data 
through complete checks or sampling. It is prioritized for its reproducibility and 
reliability.
• Indirect evaluation leverages external knowledge such as lineage, usage history, or 
expert judgment.

This evaluation framework supports consistent quality measurement across Custodians 
while reinforcing accountability and transparency.
Geospatial Data Specification
Each Custodian of a foundation Geospatial data theme develops a detailed data product 
specification. Overseen and formally approved by the National Geospatial Center, these 
specifications act as technical blueprints, defining dataset structure, content, reference 
systems, metadata requirements, and quality expectations.
Specifications are flexible in origin; they can be initiated by producers to guide new data 
collection or by users seeking derivative products. Crucially, they ensure interoperability with

Geospatial Data Quality Management
Data quality management is a lifecycle activity, spanning design, implementation, 
production, delivery, usage, and revision. At each phase, risks of misinterpretation and 
inappropriate use must be identified and managed.
This management approach is divided into three broad phases:
1. Specification Phase – Each data quality element is defined with its corresponding 
measurement approach, often re-using standardized definitions to improve 
comparability.
2. Evaluation Phase – Quality evaluation is carried out, producing both dataset quality 
outputs and metaquality assessments.

19109:2015, Geographic information — Rules for application schemas. Features 
may represent tangible objects in the world, such as roads and buildings; or con-
ceptual objects with no physical form such as administrative regions. A Feature is 
described in terms of its characteristics or properties, which can be spatial,such 
as position or extent; or non-spatial, such as name, identifier, density, or mass. 
A ‘Feature Type’ is a class of real-world objects having a common set of proper-
ties represented by attributes and associations; whereas a ‘Feature Instance’ is a 
uniquely identifiable, individual member of the Feature Type. Note that the term 
Feature may be used to denote either one of the more specific terms: Feature 
Instance or Feature Type (see [ISO 1:2014-19101]); in contexts where only one or 
the other meaning is relevant, the more specific term should be used.

Introduction
1.1 Purpose of this document
This document defines the formal KSA National Geospatial Metadata Profile for Saudi Arabia, which 
is based on the -3part ISO 19115 Metadata Standard. Its main purpose is to enable Custodians and Data 
Producers to create consistently structured metadata for all Foundation Themes.
1.2 Context
The Geospatial Foundation Theme Governance for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia requires the 
definition and implementation of a number of cross-Foundation Themes standards. The main 
reasons are:
• Discovery: To provide a common way of describing available geospatial data offerings to 
make them discoverable.
• Evaluation: To enable users to determine the fitness for purpose of existing Datasets by 
documenting quality measures and caveats indicating expected use and limitations.
• Use: To identify ways to access the data, available encodings, and available services that can 
operate on the data.
• Management: To identify what standards were used and what procedures were used to 
create and validate the data.
1.3 Intended User Groups
This document is intended as a specification for use by FTWG Custodians and Data Producers as well 
as Strategic Users.

procedures were used to 
create and validate the data.
1.3 Intended User Groups
This document is intended as a specification for use by FTWG Custodians and Data Producers as well 
as Strategic Users. It is also relevant to contractors that are required to create, update, process or validate 
geospatial metadata. An understanding of the ISO 19115 Metadata Standard and a working knowledge of 
the concepts of metadata is required.
1.4 Scope
This document specifies a set of metadata elements for describing geographic information resources. 
These resources may be datasets, dataset series, services delivering geographic data, or any other 
information resource with geospatial content. This includes datasets that relate to a limited geographic 
area. The data resources may be graphical or textual (tabular or free text), hard copy or digital.
The KSA National Geospatial Metadata Profile Standard is a profile of the 3-part ISO 19115 
Metadata Standard:
1. ISO 1:2014-19115 Geographic information – Metadata
2. ISO 2:2019-19115 Geographic information – Metadata Imagery
3. ISO 19115-3:2016 Geographic information – XML Encoding

Metadata Standard:
1. ISO 1:2014-19115 Geographic information – Metadata
2. ISO 2:2019-19115 Geographic information – Metadata Imagery
3. ISO 19115-3:2016 Geographic information – XML Encoding
As such it is entirely consistent with, and complements the requirements of all of these standards; and 
metadata conformant with this profile, will also conform to the above standards where relevant.

16
This standard does apply additional constraints, adapts the above standards to the requirements of 
KSA and provides implementation guidance (such as Arabic language support). This document does not 
specify a transfer mechanism or cataloguing service for metadata, simply the content and format of the 
metadata itself.
This document is applicable to Foundation Theme Custodians and Data Producers who are responsible 
to create and publish geospatial metadata. Although it is primarily designed for data resources held within 
KSA on a national basis, by following the principles and structures of ISO 19115 it is also applicable within 
an organization or other user community.

Metadata Standard and Profile Overview
2.1 Introduction
The Metadata Standard ISO 1-19115 specifies a mechanism (in Annex C) where a community can 
adopt relevant parts of the ISO Metadata Standard (including the ‘Core Elements’) and also extend the 
elements, keywords and Code Lists to suite that community. A Community Metadata Profile is illustrated 
in Figure 1.
This mechanism has been used to define a Metadata Profile of the 3-part ISO 19115 Metadata

keywords and Code Lists to suite that community. A Community Metadata Profile is illustrated 
in Figure 1.
This mechanism has been used to define a Metadata Profile of the 3-part ISO 19115 Metadata 
Standard for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. This chapter identifies the metadata entities and elements 
from ISO1:2014-19115, which are included in this profile and the requirements for their use.
2.1 Overview of Metadata Structure
The ISO 19115 Metadata Standard defines a series of classes (groups of information) which 
characterize different components of metadata. Figure 2 shows an overview of the main elements.
Figure 1: Community Metadata Profile

18
Figure 2: ISO 1-19115 Metadata Structure
The metadata document consists of a series of elements, some simple (such as dateInfo) and others 
more complex, such as MD_Identification (which is shown expanded) in Figure 2. This profile describes 
each of the elements in the above diagram and identifies their status in the profile (whether they 
are mandatory, and under what circumstance) and whether there are any additional implementation 
constraints or guidance in relation to the use of the elements.
The overall structure of the metadata can be thought of as two key components.
• The first component is information about the metadata itself, the date it was created, the 
metadata standard used, who created it, etc. This is because the metadata itself may be but is not 
necessarily created by the

19
Custodian.
• The second major component in the metadata is the MD_Identification element. This is the 
most complex element and describes the ‘resource’; the dataset or service the metadata is 
describing. This will potentially include a considerable amount of information about the data, its 
geographic coverage, feature content, capture precision/scale, when it was generated, etc. While 
there is a large amount of commonality, there are elements specific to Datasets and Services so 
MD_Identification has two derivatives (MD_DataIdentification and SV_ServiceIdentification) to 
capture the properties specific to these two metadata resource types.
• In addition to the MD_Identification entity, there are other complex entities in the Model (each 
leaf circle in the above diagram is a complex entity). Each of these elements will be described the 
following sections.
2.3 Additional Requirements of the KSA National Metadata Profile
This profile extends the ISO 19115 Metadata Standard in the following ways:
• Specifies Mandatory Elements. The ISO Metadata Standard only rea- quires a very limited 
set of mandatory elements. This profile adds man- datory metadata elements in specific

the following ways:

set of mandatory elements. This profile adds man- datory metadata elements in specific 
circumstances so that metadata is usable for the purposes needed. These elements are specified 
in section 4.
• Defines National Code Lists. The ISO Metadata Standard provide a number of Code Lists,

يكــون للكلمــات والعبــارات التــي تــم تعريفهــا فــي تنظيــم الهيئــة المعنــى نفســه عنــد اســتخدامها فــي هــذا الدليــل، كمــا يكــون 
للكلمــات والتعابيــر التاليــة المعانــي المقترنــة بهــا، مــا لــم يقتــض الســياق خــاف ذلــك.
 المملكة العربية السعودية.المملكة:
 الهيئة العامة للمساحة والمعلومات الجيومكانية.الهيئة:

 المركز الجيومكاني الوطني بالهيئة العامة للمساحة والمعلومات الجيومكانية.المركز:
 البيانــات الجغرافيــة المكانيــة المرتبطــة بالمــكان أو الموقــع الجغرافــي مــن إحداثيــات وحــدود المعلومــات الجيومكانيــة:
وخصائــص طبيعيــة أو صناعيــة والتــي يتــم الحصــول عليهــا عبــر وســائل تقنيــات جمــع البيانــات مثــل تقنيــات الاستشــعار عــن 
بعــد ورســم الخرائــط والمســح الأرضــي والجــوي والبحــري والمعلومــات الجيوديســية وغيرهــا مــن البيانــات.
منظومــة متكاملــة تشــمل الترتيبــات التنظيميــة للبيانــات الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة مــن البنيــة التحتيــة الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة: 
إطــار حوكمــة وأدلــة وسياســات ومعاييــر وبيانــات جيومكانيــة وطنيــة، والمــوارد البشــرية والتقنيــة الازمــة لذلــك.

ات الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة مــن البنيــة التحتيــة الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة: 
إطــار حوكمــة وأدلــة وسياســات ومعاييــر وبيانــات جيومكانيــة وطنيــة، والمــوارد البشــرية والتقنيــة الازمــة لذلــك.
 الجهــات الحكوميــة المشــاركة فــي جمــع ومعالجــة وتحليــل وتحديــث وصيانــة المعلومــات الجيومكانيــة الفئــات المســتهدفة:
التــي تقــع فــي نطــاق عملهــا وبحســب الــدور المنــاط بهــا ســواء كانــت: مســؤول تحديــث طبقــة، أو مســتخدم بيانــات، أو منتــج 
بيانــات، أو جهــة أمنيــة.
 هــي الطبقــات التــي تحتــوي علــى بيانــات جيومكانيــة تمثــل المعالــم الطبيعيــة والحضريــة الطبقــات الجيومكانيــة الأساســية:
التــي يتــم توفيرهــا مــن خال البنيــة التحتيــة الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة والتــي تربــط المعلومــات بالمــكان. ويتمكّــن المســتفيدين 
مــن الحصــول علــى قاعــدة أساســية للمعلومــات الجيومكانيــة
 هــي مجموعــة تنشــئها الهيئــة مــن الجهــات الحكوميــة والقطــاع الخــاص المشــاركة فــي انتــاج وتطويــر مجموعــة عمــل طبقــة:
البيانــات الجيومكانيــة بحســب الطبقــة الأساســية لــكل مجموعــة. ويكــون لــكل مجموعــة مســؤول تحديــث طبقــة لقيــادة

ة والقطــاع الخــاص المشــاركة فــي انتــاج وتطويــر مجموعــة عمــل طبقــة:
البيانــات الجيومكانيــة بحســب الطبقــة الأساســية لــكل مجموعــة. ويكــون لــكل مجموعــة مســؤول تحديــث طبقــة لقيــادة 
المجموعــة وأعضاءهــا بحســب الــدور المنــاط بهــم (مســتخدم بيانــات أو منتــج بيانــات أو مســؤول تحديــث طبقــة فرعيــه 
وغيــره)، ويســتضيف أمانــة المجموعــة المركــز الجيومكانــي الوطنــي بالهيئــة. 
 هــي الجهــة الحكوميــة المختصــة بتنفيــذ وصيانــة البيانــات الجيومكانيــة للطبقــة الأساســية، ويتــم مســؤول تحديــث طبقــة:
تحديدهــا مــن قبــل الهيئــة لتقــود مجموعــة عمــل تضــم ممثليــن مــن الجهــات الحكوميــة والقطــاع الخــاص التــي تــم تحديدهــا 
كمســتخدم بيانــات، ومنتــج البيانــات، ومســؤول تحديــث الطبقــة الفرعيــة والمســتخدمين ومنتجــي البيانــات للطبقــات الفرعيــة. 
 هــي الجهــة ذات العاقــة مــن القطــاع العــام أو الخــاص أو الأكاديمــي، ويتــم ترشــيحها مــن مســتخدم بيانــات جيومكانيــة:
قبــل مســؤول تحديــث الطبقــة، وتقــوم بتوفيــر المتطلبــات والاحتياجــات التــي تضمــن أن تكــون الطبقــة الأساســية أو الطبقــة 
الفرعيــة مناســبة لاحتياجــات والاســتخدامات الوطنيــة.

ومكانيــة:
قبــل مســؤول تحديــث الطبقــة، وتقــوم بتوفيــر المتطلبــات والاحتياجــات التــي تضمــن أن تكــون الطبقــة الأساســية أو الطبقــة 
الفرعيــة مناســبة لاحتياجــات والاســتخدامات الوطنيــة.
 هــي الجهــة المختصــة بتوفيــر مجموعــات البيانــات ذات الصلــة التــي تجعــل الطبقــة الأساســية منتــج بيانــات جيومكانيــة:
مناســبة ومائمــة للغــرض الــذي أنشــئت مــن أجلــه.
 هي الجهة الحكومية الأمنية المستخدمة أو المنتجة للبيانات الجيومكانية.جهة أمنية:
 هــي النافــذة للبنيــة التحتيــة الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة بالمركــز الجيومكانــي الوطنــي لتحقيــق المنصــة الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة:
أكبــر فائــدة مــن توحيــد الجهــود فــي البيانــات الجيومكانيــة وتكاملهــا بواســطة نظــام وقاعــدة بيانــات جيومكانيــة وطنيــة 
للبيانــات المتوفــرة لــدى جميــع الجهــات الحكوميــة، والاســتفادة منهــا ومشــاركتها بطريقــة ســهلة وآمنــة، ووفــق للسياســات 
الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة لحفــظ الحقــوق وتعزيــز أمــن البيانــات الجيومكانيــة.
 هــي مرجعيــة وطنيــة لمعاييــر جــودة البيانــات الجيومكانيــة وتقييــم وإدارة جودتهــا معاييــر البيانــات الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة:

وطنيــة لحفــظ الحقــوق وتعزيــز أمــن البيانــات الجيومكانيــة.
 هــي مرجعيــة وطنيــة لمعاييــر جــودة البيانــات الجيومكانيــة وتقييــم وإدارة جودتهــا معاييــر البيانــات الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة:
والمواصفــات القياســية للبيانــات الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة، ومعاييــر جمــع وتوثيــق وصيانــة وتحديــث البيانــات الجيومكانيــة 
الوطنيــة.
نظــام مرجعــي ثابــت معتمــد مــن الهيئــة يحــدد الإحداثيــات الكارتيزيــة وخطــوط الطــول ودوائــر المرجــع المكانــي الوطنــي: 
العــرض والارتفــاع والمقيــاس والجاذبيــة والتوجيــه فــي جميــع أنحــاء المملكــة.
 هــي مرجعيــة وطنيــة لمبــادئ حوكمــة البيانــات الجيومكانيــة وسياســة تصنيــف سياســات البيانــات الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة:
وتســعير وترخيــص ومشــاركة والمحافظــة علــى البيانــات الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة.

مسؤولية تحديث البيانات:
 يجــب أن تكــون هنــاك جهــة مســؤولة عــن جمــع البيانــات، وضمــان جــودة البيانــات ومعالجــة المســؤوليات القانونيــة المترتبــة 
عليهــا، بحســب إطــار حوكمــة البيانــات الجيومكانيــة المعتمــد.
IDتعيين المعرّف
 يعد تحديد هوية فريدة، وثابتة، عملية ضرورية لتعريف البيانات وإمكانية تتبعها بمرور الوقت.
صلاحية البيانات المحددة:
 يجــب وضــع مواصفــات لتحديــد جــودة البيانــات، بحيــث تــدل المعاييــر الواضحــة لصحــة البيانــات ودقتهــا علــى ضمــان موثوقيــة 
البيانات.
توثيق البيانات: 
يجــب إعــداد البيانــات الوصفيــة، ومعلومــات مصــدر البيانــات الجيومكانيــة لدعــم التحقــق منهــا، حيــث ان توثيــق مصــادر البيانــات، 
وخطــوات المعالجــة يســاعد فــي بنــاء موثوقيــة البيانــات.
ضمان جودة البيانات:
 تســاعد إجــراءات ضمــان الجــودة علــى بنــاء الثقــة فــي جــودة البيانــات، كمــا يمكــن اســتخدام تقنيــات الــذكاء الاصطناعــي فــي 
التحقــق مــن دقــة البيانــات وســامتها والتحقــق منهــا.
عملية تقييم الجودة:

ضمــان الجــودة علــى بنــاء الثقــة فــي جــودة البيانــات، كمــا يمكــن اســتخدام تقنيــات الــذكاء الاصطناعــي فــي 
التحقــق مــن دقــة البيانــات وســامتها والتحقــق منهــا.
عملية تقييم الجودة:
 تشــمل عمليــة تقيــم الجــودة عناصــر جــودة البيانــات مثــل: الاكتمــال، والدقــة المكانيــة، والجــودة الموضوعيــة، والامتثــال 
لمواصفــات البيانــات. 
جمع عناصر المراقبة: 
يجب توثيق تفاصيل المراقبة بشكل صحيح، لتقييم ما إذا كانت البيانات مناسبة للتطبيقات من عدمه.
 الثقة في البيانات: 
يجب توفير معلومات مصدر البيانات، لضمان صحة البيانات ونزاهتها.

للحفــاظ علــى البيانــات الجيومكانيــة وصيانتهــا وتحديثهــا ، يجــب وضــع خطــط لضمــان صيانــة وتحديــث البيانــات الجيومكانيــة، 
تشــمل الإجــراءات والمواصفــات والتمويــل لصيانــة البيانــات المنتجــة، ويجــب اتبــاع المبــادئ الاساســية التاليــة لصيانة وتحديث 
البيانــات الجيومكانية:
التزامن للحفاظ على البيانات وصيانتها. 
التحقــق مــن ان البيانــات الجيومكانيــة لا تــزال ذات قيمــة بوضعهــا الراهــن ولــم تتقــادم بمــا وقــع عليهــا مــن تغيــرات 
بمــرور الزمــن.
أن تكــون تحديثــات البيانــات الجيومكانيــة علــى فتــرات منتظمــة أو عنــد اكتشــاف التغييــرات التــي تتجــاوز مقــدار

استمرارية قياس ما إذا كانت فترات التحديث متزامنة مع وتيرة التغييرات التي تحدث في الواقع بشكل دوري.

ولمزيــد مــن التفاصيــل حــول تلــك المعاييــر، يمكــن الوصــول الــى ســجل معاييــر البيانــات الجيومكانيــة الوطنيــة عــن طريــق الدخــول علــى
